title: A pricing page for a creative studio
metaTitle: Creative studio pricing page: show the fit
excerpt: Use the pricing page to judge fit: what is included, what is not, and how to start. Do not hide the shape of the price if the buyer will ask anyway.
alt: A silver laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, with a monitor, mug, and phone behind it, as plain as a pricing page ought to be.
caption: A laptop, a monitor, a mug, and a phone on a white desk. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Do you have to publish exact prices?
faqs.answer: You have to publish the shape. A fixed project for a defined site, a partnership when the work keeps changing, or a first step when the brief is still unknown. A range you will honor is more trustworthy than a number you abandon on the first call, and better than a blank contact line.

faqs.question: What belongs on the not-included list?
faqs.answer: The surprises that usually show up later. A photoshoot, paid media, a second product, copy for the whole company, or changes after launch if they are not in the partnership. Naming them is how a buyer trusts the included list.

faqs.question: How many pricing options should a studio show?
faqs.answer: Two clear ways are usually enough: a defined project and an ongoing partnership. Add a third only if you truly sell it. Five columns that differ by adjectives force the buyer to decode your packaging.

markdown:
A creative studio pricing page is where a client who has already seen fifty portfolios decides whether the work fits, not where they do arithmetic. Show what is included, what is not, and how to start a project.

Do not hide the shape of the price if the buyer will ask anyway. A blank "contact us" block tells a skeptical client that the number is a surprise, or that the studio has not decided what it sells.

## Fit before the calculator

The buyer arriving here has usually already seen a decision in the work. They are asking a narrower question. Is a project of that kind something I can commission, and is the boundary one I understand? If the page opens with a manifesto about value, it answers a question they did not bring.

Write the first lines as a map. Two or three ways to work together. Who each one is for. What each one refuses. The amounts can sit under that map. The map is the part that earns the rest of the visit. [Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page helps someone complete a real task. Pricing is a task. A page that withholds the shape of the offer fails it.

Name the buyer in their words. A founder who needs a site before a raise. A brand lead who needs a system a small team will actually use. A shop that needs the store rebuilt without a week of broken checkout. If none of your lines sound like a person, the tiers are still internal categories.

Keep the page calm. No countdown. No "most popular" badge on the tier you wish people would buy, unless you can say why it is the common fit. Decoration that pushes a package is a tell. This client has seen it on fifty other sites.

## The shape of the price

You do not have to publish a single number for every possible brief. You do have to show the shape. A fixed project for a defined site. A longer partnership when the product keeps changing. A conversation first when the work is genuinely unknown, with a sentence that says what would make it knowable.

A fixed project should say what "defined" means. A marketing site with a set of pages. A brand system small enough to use. A store migration with a list of what moves. If the definition is "it depends," you do not have a fixed project yet, and you should not draw a box that pretends you do.

A partnership should say the cadence and the kind of decisions it covers. A monthly block for a product that is still finding its screens. Design and build together, so the files do not wait on a second vendor. It should also say what a quiet month looks like. Clients fear retainers that bill the same when nothing ships.

When the work is unknown, say so in one sentence and offer the smallest step that makes it known. A short call. A paid working session. A written scope after that. Hiding behind "custom quote" with no step is how serious buyers leave to email a studio that showed the shape.

Do not invent precision you cannot keep. A range is more trustworthy than a number you will abandon on the first call. If your projects cluster, show the cluster. If they do not, say that the price follows pages, states, and the number of decisions, and show one worked example so the method is visible.

## What is included, and what is not

Each offer needs an included list and a not-included list. The second list is the one that builds trust. Clients who have hired before have been surprised by photography, by a second language, by copy, by the cost of a font, by a CMS nobody on the team could edit.

Included, for a typical site engagement, should be concrete. The pages in the scope. Design in a tool the team can open, such as Figma. A production front end. A way to edit the words that change. Launch checks for speed, basic accessibility, and the domain. A place where brand files, notes, and updates live after delivery. On a Hanabi project that place is the client portal.

Not included should be just as concrete. A photoshoot. Paid media. Illustration beyond the system you agreed. A second product. Writing the entire company voice if the engagement was a site. Ongoing changes after launch, unless the partnership tier says otherwise. Naming these is not a lack of generosity. It is the boundary that keeps the date real.

Revisions need one line. How many rounds are in the price, and what a round is. "Unlimited revisions" on a studio site usually means the scope was never written down. A clear round, tied to a decision, is easier to buy than a vague promise of endless polish.

Ownership needs one line too. The client should leave with the repository, the domain, and the content logins. Say that on the pricing page. A buyer who has been locked out of a previous site is reading for this sentence.

## How many ways to buy

Two clear ways beat five decorative tiers. A defined project and an ongoing partnership cover most studios. A third line for advisory, or for a small brand system before the site, is enough if you actually sell it. Five columns that differ by adjectives ("basic," "growth," "premium") ask the buyer to decode your packaging.

If you use columns, make the differences factual. Number of pages. Whether engineering is included. Whether the brand system is included. Response expectations you can keep. Do not make the differences atmospheric. "More strategy" is not a line item.

Order the offers the way a client qualifies themselves. The defined project first if that is what most buyers need. The partnership second, with a sentence about when it is the better fit. Do not lead with the largest number because it flatters the studio.

A short note under the columns can say what changes the price without turning into a lawyer's appendix. More templates. A store. A content model. A language. An integration. One sentence each. The buyer should see that you have priced these before, even if today's figure is a conversation.

## The questions a skeptical client brings

Answer the questions they will ask on the call, on the page, in plain sentences.

What do you need from us before a number is real? Access to the current site, a rough page list, and the decision the project has to get right. What you do not need is a finished brief in agency format.

How do we start? One action. Start a project. The button should go to a short path, not to a ten-field form that repeats the page.

Who does the work? If the same people design and build, say that. If a specialist joins for motion or for a store, say when. Hanabi designs and builds in the open stack a founder can keep: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and, when the product needs data, Prisma and PostgreSQL on Vercel. Name the true shape of your own team. Do not borrow a stack as decoration.

What does a week feel like? A working rhythm they can picture. Shared files. A place comments land. A decision recorded so the next round does not restart. You do not need to publish an internal process diagram. You need the buyer to know they will not be guessing.

When do you say no? A line about the work you do not take protects both sides. If you do not do brand-only projects, or you do not take marketplaces, say it near the price. The client who is a poor fit will leave earlier, which is the point of a pricing page.

## Where the page should send them

The pricing page should end on the work, not on a second essay about craft. They judged fit from the shape. They confirm it by seeing a project with a constraint and a decision. Point them at two pieces that match the tiers you just described. A defined site. A longer product engagement. Captions, not a reel.

Selected work is the check on the number. If you want to see how a studio shows that check, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and notice which projects carry a decision rather than a mood. Then hold your own pricing page to the same standard. The tier and the project should describe the same kind of job.

Before you publish, read the page as the client. Can you tell what is included, what is not, and how to start, without booking the call first? If the answer is no, the page is still a tease. Add the missing boundary. Do not add another adjective.

The offer list itself is the next page to write if the tiers still sound like internal names. A [services page for a creative studio](/blog/the-services-page-a-creative-studio-actually-needs) puts each kind of work in the buyer's language, with an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. Pricing says the shape. Services say the job. They should not be the same paragraph copied twice.
